newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: OPINION - Where the real power lies.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - Where the real power lies.

text.p: By Peter Jolly, Economist, Bank of New Zealand.

WELLINGTON, Nov 8 - Lamenting on the loss of power for government, given the increasing ability of the world's capital markets to deliver real costs to a government with astray policy or profligate expenditure plans, President Clinton's campaign director, James Carville, was moved to say "I used to think that if there was reincarnation, I wanted to come back as the President, or the Pope. But now I want to be the bond market -- you can intimidate everybody".
James Carville was only partially right, for he forgot where the real power now lies -- central banks.
The gradual transferral of the monetary policy levers away from elected politicians to central bankers has sped up over the past decade.

Arguably, this new power for central banks will approach its zenith at the beginning of 1999, if most European countries pass sovereignty over the value of their currency, and by implication monetary policy, to the new European Central Bank by way of fixing their exchange rates within EMU.

While New Zealand politicians have remained in huddled coalition negotiations since the October 12 general election, the important job of overseeing the economy's progress goes on regardless, with the Reserve Bank at the helm and tweaking the policy levers a couple of times in recent weeks.
Strong performances by all New Zealand financial markets since the election is recognition this transition of power to the central bank is well understood.

The Reserve Bank has also found time to flex their muscles at the huddled politicians, in their "Briefing on the Reserve Bank of New Zealand", released a couple of weeks ago to politicians and the public.

Amid coalition negotiations where it is perhaps the final bill for expenditure initiatives that is most important for markets and monetary policy, the Reserve Bank noted that "...when fiscal policy stimulates aggregate demand through additional expenditures or tax cuts, as is now the case, monetary policy will need to assume a firmer stance than would otherwise be required to prevent the fiscal policy stimulus from
feeding through to inflation".
No great revelations here, but certainly an assurance to the huddled politicians that they face a fiscal/monetary policy trade-off when the huddle breaks.
This new power for the central bank is under no real threat from the huddled politicians.

A large majority of the new parliament support the "three pillars" of the current monetary policy framework the RBNZ highlighted in the "briefing" document, namely: "the specification of a clear policy objective, the delegation to the Bank of the autonomy to pursue this objective, and the
requirement of transparency on the conduct of policy".
There only remains a question over what the new inflation target will be.
On the subject of a new target range the "briefing" is less than forthcoming.
On the one hand, the "briefing" notes that the Policy Targets Agreement (PTA), which sets the bank's specific objective of 0-2 percent inflation, is not set in stone and will evolve through time.
On the other hand, the discussion in the "briefing" goes on to endorse the current inflation target and measure.
The process of "evolution", it seems, will not be led by the Reserve Bank, but rather the politicians -- some power at last!

At this stage, the 0-2 percent inflation target seems assured of going, whoever forms the government, with contenders for its replacement being: -1 to 3 percent, 0 to 3 percent, to perhaps even 0 to 4 percent.

Also, some minor changes to the target inflation measures are likely, with the regular removal of government charges, tax changes, and volatile fresh fruit and vegetable prices -- all of which have helped to cause target breaches in the past -- seeming sensible.

However, on the implications of a wider band the Reserve Bank did note that "If the Bank were given greater latitude in the formulation of policy, there would be a real possibility that this latitude would be used".
So slightly easier policy could be expected now if the band was wider, even though the midpoint is the same.

Of course, this is a double edged sword, for as the RBNZ also noted, a wider band "would likely lead to inflation outcomes near the top of the range than near the bottom of the range, and average inflation correspondingly higher".

A flattener of the current inverted yield curve too be sure. So the Reserve Bank may face a slightly easier inflation target but at the same time they may face more expansive fiscal policy when the government is formed.

Should the politicians remain huddled for much longer, uncertainty over the magnitude and the timing of these two impacts, along with the usual difficulties of assessing the likely path for the economy, will make the writing of the Reserve Bank's December 17 Monetary Statement especially challenging.
The economy itself has been softer over the past quarter, in line with the Reserve Bank's September Economic Projections, yet the September quarter inflation result was markedly better than expected.

While overall monetary conditions have been at least as firm as assumed, the combination of higher currency and lower interest rates will have improved prospects for domestic demand at the expense of the external sector contributing to growth.

As in September the Reserve Bank were building in some easing of monetary conditions over their forecast horizon anyway (ala the flat TWI assumption), the case for an easing of monetary policy in December can clearly be built, particularly if the inflation band is widened.
Markets are already anticipating this.

However, if the Reserve Bank were to believe the anticipated economic recovery looks on track, and that recent mortgage interest rate falls will provide a timely boost to the inflationary housing market, and more expansionary fiscal policy seems assured, then the cautious approach of merely sanctioning
the higher currency and the fall in interest rates to date, would seem sensible.
The Bank of New Zealand's approach would be the latter, for we expect the economy will recover over the summer and into 1997, meaning inflation will not fall far, nor sustainably through 1997.
When the huddled politicians break could be crucial.

An early announcement of a new inflation target band seems likely, when the full scale of additional fiscal expenditure may not become clear until the release of the government's Budget Policy Statement in February.
This may require the Reserve Bank to be at first accommodating, and to be less so in the New Year.
They may have a lot of power, but probably also quite a few headaches.
(Note - The opinions expressed in this article represent the views of the author only. They should not be seen as reflecting the views of Reuters.)
